meta.title: Chat Messaging
meta.summary: 1:1 and group messaging (WhatsApp / Messenger style) over persistent connections, with offline delivery, push notifications and encrypted media.

functional: Send photos, voice notes and files up to ~100 MB
Offline users get a push notification and receive missed messages on reconnect
Message history syncs across a user's devices
nonFunctional: Delivery < 500 ms when both users are online
No message is ever lost once the sender sees ✓
Messages appear in the same order for everyone in a conversation

scale.label: Media
scale.value: ~10% of messages carry a file (~4B/day, mostly < 1 MB)

slos.name: Delivery speed
slos.sli: Messages delivered to an online recipient within the threshold, divided by all such messages, from send to delivery acknowledgement

slos.name: No message lost
slos.sli: Acknowledged messages that can still be read, divided by acknowledged messages

slos.name: Connection availability
slos.sli: Connection attempts that succeed, divided by all attempts, at the load balancer

alerts.when: p99 delivery latency above 500 ms for 10 minutes
alerts.why: Chat that is not instant feels broken.

alerts.when: Message store cannot reach write quorum
alerts.why: Writes are failing, and acknowledged messages are at risk.

alerts.when: Connection failures burning the error budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
Connections per gateway above 80% of the limit
alerts.why: Add gateways before a node hits its limit and drops its users.

alerts.when: Oldest push queue message above 60 seconds
alerts.why: Offline users learn about messages late.

alerts.when: Registered sessions differ from open connections by more than 2%
alerts.why: Messages get routed to gateways that no longer hold the user.

signals.name: Disconnects by reason
signals.why: Separates network problems from deploys and overload.

signals.name: Registered sessions against open connections
signals.why: Drift means stale entries or missed heartbeats.

signals.name: Write quorum failures
signals.why: The earliest sign that durability is at risk.

signals.name: Upload failures
signals.why: Shows whether signed URLs or storage are the problem.

steps: Break delivery latency down by step: store write, session lookup or gateway hop.
Check message store write latency and quorum errors.
Check the session registry hit rate: a miss sends the message down the offline path.
Check gateway CPU and connection counts.
Check the push queue age and worker errors.
Check provider responses: unregistered tokens (410) should be removed.

nodes.label: Network Load Balancer
nodes.description: Layer 4: passes long-lived TCP connections straight to the gateways

nodes.label: Chat Gateway
nodes.description: Terminates WebSockets; each node holds ~1M connections

nodes.label: Session Registry
nodes.description: user → gateway node holding their connection, with a heartbeat TTL

nodes.label: Message Store
nodes.description: Cassandra-style: partition = conversation, clustering = message id

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.description: Geo / latency routed: sends each client to the nearest region's load balancer

nodes.label: CDN (media)
nodes.description: Caches encrypted media near recipients; chat traffic never goes through it

nodes.label: Media Storage
nodes.description: Encrypted images, videos, voice notes and files

flows.title: Connect and go online
flows.summary: Resolve the service, open one long-lived connection, and register which gateway holds it so messages can find this user.

steps.label: resolve chat.example.com
steps.detail: Clients look the service up by name, and DNS answers with the nearest region's load balancer (geo or latency routing). A short TTL (about 60 s) lets traffic move away from a failing region. This happens once per connect, not per message.

steps.label: NLB address (nearest region)
steps.detail: Apps also ship a fallback hostname and a list of IPs, because DNS can be slow or blocked on some networks.

steps.label: TCP + TLS + WebSocket upgrade
steps.detail: One connection stays open for hours, so the cost of setting it up is paid once. The layer-4 balancer just passes the bytes through.
steps.payload:
GET /ws HTTP/1.1
Upgrade: websocket
Authorization: Bearer eyJ…

steps.label: pick a gateway (least connections)
steps.detail: Spreading connections evenly matters more than spreading requests: each gateway holds about a million sockets.

steps.label: authenticate + register
steps.detail: The gateway checks the token, then tells the message service this user is online here.

steps.label: SET session:alice gateway-17 EX 60
steps.detail: This entry is how every later message finds Alice. The gateway refreshes it with a heartbeat every 30 s, so if the gateway dies the entry expires within a minute and she is treated as offline.

steps.label: connected
steps.detail: From here Alice can send and receive over the same socket. The client reconnects automatically with backoff and jitter, so a gateway restart does not cause a stampede.

flows.title: Send (recipient online)
flows.summary: Persist first, acknowledge the sender, then route to the exact gateway holding the recipient's connection.

steps.label: WS frame: send
steps.detail: The client generates its own message id so a resend after a dropped connection can be deduplicated.

steps.label: same TCP connection
steps.detail: A layer-4 balancer just pins connections; the gateway terminates the WebSocket.

steps.label: INSERT (QUORUM)
steps.detail: Write before delivering: if anything crashes after this, the message still exists. A quorum write survives one replica being down.
steps.payload:
INSERT INTO messages (conv_id, msg_id, sender, body)
VALUES ('c_alice_bob', 0x18f3…, 'alice', <ciphertext>)
IF NOT EXISTS;  -- dedupe on client_msg_id

steps.label: OK, msg_id
steps.detail: The time-sortable msg_id fixes the order within the conversation for every reader.

steps.label: ✓ sent
steps.detail: Alice's single tick means: stored on the server, will not be lost.

steps.label: gateway-17
steps.detail: Bob is online; his connection lives on gateway node 17.

steps.label: deliver via gateway-17
steps.detail: Internal RPC straight to the node that holds Bob's socket. No broadcast to all gateways.

steps.label: delivered(msg_id)
steps.detail: Relayed to Alice the same way, turning ✓ into ✓✓.

flows.title: Send (recipient offline)
flows.summary: Store, notify through APNs/FCM, and let the recipient pull missed messages when they reconnect.

steps.label: INSERT (QUORUM)
steps.detail: The message store is also the offline inbox: nothing extra to keep in sync.

steps.label: (none)
steps.detail: No heartbeat for 60 s, so the session entry expired: Bob is offline.

steps.label: enqueue push
steps.detail: Push providers are slow and rate-limited; a queue keeps them off the send path.

steps.label: send notification
steps.detail: With end-to-end encryption the push carries no message text, just "New message" and a conversation id.

steps.label: sync since cursor
steps.detail: The gateway also registers Bob in the session registry again.

steps.label: SELECT msg_id > cursor
steps.detail: One partition read per conversation, already sorted by msg_id.

flows.title: Send an image
flows.summary: Media skips the chat servers: it goes straight to object storage with a short-lived signed URL, and the message carries only a reference. The recipient downloads it through a CDN.

steps.label: encrypt on device
steps.detail: The file is encrypted with a fresh random key before it leaves the phone. The key travels inside the end-to-end encrypted message, so storage and the CDN only ever see ciphertext.

steps.label: WS frame: request upload
steps.detail: Alice asks for an upload slot over her open connection.

steps.label: sign upload URL
steps.detail: The service signs a PUT URL locally with its storage credentials: it expires in 5 minutes and is bound to this size and content type. Nothing is sent to storage yet.

steps.label: upload slot
steps.detail: A 5 MB photo never touches the chat servers, which stay free for messages.

steps.label: PUT ciphertext (direct)
steps.detail: Gigabytes per second of uploads go straight to object storage. A failed upload is retried on its own, without resending a message.

steps.label: WS frame: send (media ref)
steps.detail: Now the ordinary message: text plus a reference to the file and its decryption key (inside the encrypted body).

steps.label: HEAD m/8c1f
steps.detail: Before accepting the message, check the file really arrived and its size matches. Otherwise Bob would get a message pointing at nothing.

steps.label: INSERT (QUORUM)
steps.detail: The message is stored like any other; only its body differs.

steps.label: ✓ sent
steps.detail: Delivery to Bob works exactly as in "Send (recipient online)" and is not repeated here.

steps.label: message arrives with a media reference
steps.detail: Bob sees a blurred thumbnail (sent inline in the message) while the full file downloads.

steps.label: GET /m/8c1f
steps.detail: Downloads use a plain HTTPS URL on the CDN, not the chat connection.

steps.label: MISS
steps.detail: First recipient in this region. In a group chat, everyone after Bob gets a HIT, so the file leaves origin storage once.

steps.label: ciphertext
steps.detail: The CDN caches the ciphertext. It cannot read it, and storage lifecycle rules delete it after about 30 days.

steps.label: decrypt with the key from the message
steps.detail: Only Bob and Alice hold the key.

notes.text: Partition by conversation so one conversation's history is a single sorted read. Very large groups need bucketing (conv_id + month) to keep partitions bounded.
Quorum reads and writes across 3 zones keep working with one zone down; the cluster still has 2 of 3 replicas.
If a gateway node dies, its clients reconnect to another node and re-register. Messages sent in between wait in the store and arrive on sync.
WebSockets give instant delivery; long polling is simpler but costs far more requests. Gateways must drain connections gradually on deploys to avoid reconnect storms.
End-to-end encryption (Signal protocol): the server stores and routes ciphertext only and never sees message content.
Groups: small groups fan out on write (one delivery per member). Large broadcast channels switch to fan-out on read.

Geo or latency routing keeps each user in the nearest region and lets you shift traffic away from a failing one. TTLs are short (about 60 s) for that reason; clients also keep fallback hostnames and IPs.
Sending media through the chat servers would tie up gateway connections and bandwidth. Direct-to-storage upload with signed URLs scales independently and makes uploads resumable.
Chat traffic is unique, long-lived connections, so a CDN cannot help there. It only serves media downloads, where one group photo is fetched by many recipients.

questions.q: How do you keep messages in the right order within a conversation?
questions.a: Assign a per-conversation sequence number on the server when the message is stored, not the client's clock. Clients display by that sequence and can detect gaps. Ordering across different conversations does not matter, which is what lets you partition the message store by conversation.

questions.q: Bob is offline when Alice sends a message. How does he get it?
questions.a: The message is stored first, so it is never lost. Because Bob has no live connection in the session registry, a push notification job goes on the queue and the workers send it through APNs or FCM. When Bob opens the app it syncs everything after the last sequence number it saw.

questions.q: How do you make sure a message is delivered exactly once even with retries?
questions.a: Delivery is at least once and display is exactly once. The client attaches a unique message id, the server stores it idempotently so a retry does not create a duplicate, and the recipient ignores ids it has already shown. Acks for sent, delivered and read are separate events on the same id.

questions.q: With millions of connections across many gateways, how does a message find the recipient's connection?
questions.a: The session registry maps each online user to the gateway holding their connection. The message service looks up Bob's gateway and forwards to it, or publishes on a channel that gateway subscribes to. Entries are refreshed by heartbeats and expire so a dead gateway does not keep stale routes.

questions.q: How does group chat change the design, especially for very large groups?
questions.a: Store a group message once and fan out only the delivery: look up members and push to those online, notify the rest. For large groups, avoid per-member writes and let clients pull by sequence number. Cap group size or switch very large groups to a broadcast or channel model.

questions.q: How are images and videos sent without overloading the chat servers?
questions.a: The sender uploads the file directly to object storage with a signed URL and the message carries only a reference and a small thumbnail. Recipients download it through the CDN. Chat servers only handle small messages, which keeps connection handling fast.
